Proxy-SVAR (external instrument) identification and bootstrap inference

Source: R/psvar.R
varm_proxy.Rd

Mertens & Ravn (2013) / Stock & Watson (2012) proxy identification of r structural shocks in a reduced-form varm() fit, using r external instruments. With one instrument the impact vector is \(\gamma = T^{-1}\sum_t u_t m_t\) (covariance of the reduced-form residuals with the proxy), scaled so that the impact response of target equals size. Responses are \(\Theta_h \gamma\), reusing the MA machinery of irf(). With r > 1 instruments the Mertens-Ravn (2013) B11/B21 formulae are used (see Details).

Usage

varm_proxy(
  fit,
  m,
  target = 1L,
  size = 1,
  horizon = 20L,
  nboot = 500L,
  level = c(0.68, 0.9),
  method = c("mbb", "wild", "wild_normal"),
  block = NULL
)

Arguments

fit

a varm() object.

m

proxy: numeric vector, or T x r matrix of r proxies, aligned with the data (the first p rows are dropped to match the residuals).

target

variable(s) (name or position) whose impact response is normalised to size; length r.

size

size of the shock (impact response of target); scalar or length r.

horizon

maximum horizon (impact is 0).

nboot

number of bootstrap draws (0 for point estimates only).

level

confidence levels; bands are equal-tailed percentiles.

method

"mbb" (default), "wild" or "wild_normal"; see Details.

block

moving-block length for method = "mbb" (default Jentsch-Lunsford rule).

Value

a varm_proxy object. For r = 1: estimate ((H+1) x K), draws ((H+1) x K x nboot), bands ((H+1) x K x 2*length(level)). For r > 1 each gains a shock dimension after K. Also gamma (impact covariance with the proxy), fstat (see proxy_fstat()), B1 (unit-variance impact matrix, NULL if not computable), shocks, reliability, method, block.

Details

Inference (method).

"wild"

Mertens & Ravn (2013) / Gertler & Karadi (2015)-style recursive-design wild bootstrap: Rademacher weights multiply the residuals and the proxy jointly.

"wild_normal"

same with standard-normal weights (the other variant studied by Jentsch & Lunsford).

"mbb"

residual-based moving block bootstrap of Jentsch & Lunsford: blocks of length block are drawn jointly from the residuals and the proxy, each is recentred by the mean of the corresponding within-block position over all blocks, the VAR is re-simulated recursively and re-estimated. Block length default is the Jentsch-Lunsford rule \(\ell = 5.03\,T^{1/4}\) (\(\ell = 20\) at \(T = 250\)).

Jentsch & Lunsford (2019, 2022) show that the wild bootstrap is asymptotically invalid for proxy-SVAR impulse responses, because multiplying residuals and proxy by the same weight leaves the sample covariance \(T^{-1}\sum m_t u_t'\) (almost) fixed, so the sampling variability of the impact vector is not reproduced, and that the moving block bootstrap is valid. Mertens & Ravn (2019) dispute the practical conclusions. The wild bootstrap remains available (method = "wild") to reproduce Mertens-Ravn / Gertler-Karadi bands. The default changed from "wild" to "mbb" on the strength of that theory and of the Monte Carlo in validation/proxy-coverage.R (wild-bootstrap 90% coverage of the impact response of a non-target variable was about 14% vs 87% for the block bootstrap). Neither bootstrap is robust to weak instruments (varm_proxy_robust() is). Intervals are equal-tailed percentiles, as in the papers.

Several instruments. m may be a T x r matrix and target a vector of r variables: r instruments identify r shocks. As in the Mertens-Ravn algorithm (and the SVAR-IV MATLAB code of Miranda-Agrippino), the shocks are identified up to a Cholesky-type restriction within the block of target variables, so the order of target matters. The impact matrix is normalised so that column i has impact size[i] on target[i]. Missing instrument values must be zero-filled (this leaves the normalised responses unchanged); NA are rejected.

The extra output shocks (realised unit-variance structural shocks, \(\varepsilon_t = B_1'\Sigma_u^{-1}u_t\)) and reliability (squared correlation of the instrument with the shock; squared canonical correlations if r > 1) are sample objects computed from the point estimates, valid when the instrument is relevant and exogenous; no censoring adjustment is made.

References

Mertens, K. and Ravn, M. O. (2013). The dynamic effects of personal and corporate income tax changes in the United States. AER 103(4), 1212-1247.

Jentsch, C. and Lunsford, K. G. (2019). The dynamic effects of personal and corporate income tax changes in the United States: comment. AER 109(7), 2655-2678.

Jentsch, C. and Lunsford, K. G. (2022). Asymptotically valid bootstrap inference for proxy SVARs. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics (2022; working paper version: Cleveland Fed WP 16-19).

See also

varm_proxy_robust(), varm_proxy_bayes(), lp() (LP-IV)

Examples

set.seed(1)
e <- matrix(rnorm(400), 200)
y <- matrix(0, 200, 2)
for (t in 2:200) y[t, ] <- 0.5 * y[t - 1, ] + c(e[t, 1] + 0.3 * e[t, 2], e[t, 2] + 0.5 * e[t, 1])
fit <- varm(y, p = 1)
varm_proxy(fit, m = e[, 1] + rnorm(200, sd = 0.5), horizon = 8, nboot = 100)
#> <varm_proxy> shock to y1 (size 1), horizon 0..8, 100 moving-block-bootstrap draws (block length 19)
#> first-stage F = 428.8; robust F = 441.7
#> instrument reliability: 0.766
varm_proxy(fit, m = e[, 1] + rnorm(200, sd = 0.5), horizon = 8, nboot = 100, method = "mbb")
#> <varm_proxy> shock to y1 (size 1), horizon 0..8, 100 moving-block-bootstrap draws (block length 19)
#> first-stage F = 520.8; robust F = 495.9
#> instrument reliability: 0.789
